content: 1. Evidence synthesis, validation, informativeness, country ownership, iteration, relevance, realism, appropriateness, transparency, timeliness, and evidence synthesis are critical components in country-level tuberculosis (TB) modeling. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) introduced the End TB Strategy in 2015, which outlines a comprehensive approach to ending the global TB epidemic. This strategy emphasizes the importance of country ownership, evidence-based interventions, and iterative processes to achieve its goals. 3. The Stop TB Partnership developed the Global Plan to End TB (2016–2020), which provides a roadmap for implementing the End TB Strategy. This plan highlights the need for collaboration, innovation, and resource mobilization to combat TB effectively. 4. The WHO's Global Tuberculosis Report (2017) provides detailed data on the global TB burden, progress toward targets, and areas requiring urgent attention. This report serves as a critical resource for policymakers and researchers. 5. Rapid molecular diagnostic tools, such as those described by Boehme et al. (2010), have revolutionized TB detection and rifampin resistance testing, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and timeliness. 6. Novel treatments, such as the diarylquinoline TMC207 (described by Diacon et al., 2009) and delamanid (described by Gler et al., 2012), have shown promise in treating multidrug-resistant TB, offering new hope for patients with limited treatment options. 7. Mathematical modeling studies, such as those by Eaton et al. (2014) and Houben et al. (2016), have demonstrated the potential health benefits, cost-effectiveness, and feasibility of achieving global TB targets through expanded treatment coverage and policy changes. 8. Cost-effectiveness analyses, such as those by Menzies et al. These studies provide valuable insights for optimizing resource allocation. 9. Methodological advancements in health services research, such as constrained optimization methods (Crown et al., 2017) and state-transition modeling (Siebert et al., 2012), have enhanced the rigor and applicability of economic evaluations in TB and other health interventions. 10. The International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research (ISPOR) has published guidelines on good research practices for modeling, including transparency, validation, and uncertainty analysis (Briggs et al., 2012; Eddy et al., 2012). 11. The Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards (CHEERS) provide a framework for reporting health economic evaluations, promoting consistency and clarity in the presentation of findings (Husereau et al., 2013). 12. The International Decision Support Initiative (iDSI) Reference Case offers guidance on conducting economic evaluations to inform health policy decisions, emphasizing the importance of context-specific analyses (Wilkinson et al., 2016). 13. Studies on HIV treatment as prevention, such as those by Delva et al. (2015), highlight the importance of optimizing the impact of expanded HIV treatment programs on TB outcomes, particularly in high-burden settings. 14. Economic analyses of HPV vaccination in lowand middle-income countries, as described by Jit et al. (2011, 2013), provide valuable guidance for decision-making on vaccine introduction and implementation. 15. Methodological considerations for economic modeling of latent TB infection screening in migrants, as discussed by Shedrawy et al. (2017), underscore the complexity of evaluating interventions in diverse populations. These references collectively provide a comprehensive foundation for advancing TB modeling, economic evaluations, and health policy decision-making.
